title: Oscillations in Physics
short_intro: Oscillations refer to periodic motions of a physical system about an equilibrium position, typically governed by a linear restoring force. They form the foundational mechanics for understanding wave phenomena, acoustics, and alternating current circuits.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) kinematics, dynamics, energy conservation, simple pendulum, and spring-mass systems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Damped and forced oscillations, resonance, phase portraits, superposition of orthogonal oscillations (Lissajous figures), and Fourier analysis of periodic waveforms.

prerequisites: Newton's laws of motion and rotational dynamics
Differential equations of second order with constant coefficients

concept_notes.heading: Kinematics of Simple Harmonic Motion
bullets: Displacement in SHM is given by x(t) = A sin(ωt + φ), where A is amplitude, ω is angular frequency, and φ is initial phase.
Velocity v(t) = dx/dt = Aω cos(ωt + φ) leads to the velocity-displacement relation v = ω √(A<sup>2</sup> - x<sup>2</sup>).
Acceleration a(t) = dv/dt = -ω<sup>2</sup>x demonstrates that acceleration is directly proportional to displacement and oppositely directed.

concept_notes.heading: Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
bullets: Potential energy (U) stored in a spring of stiffness k is U = (1/2)kx<sup>2</sup> = (1/2)mω<sup>2</sup>A<sup>2</sup> sin<sup>2</sup>(ωt + φ).
Kinetic energy (K) of the oscillating mass is K = (1/2)mv<sup>2</sup> = (1/2)mω<sup>2</sup>A<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup>(ωt + φ).
Total mechanical energy E = U + K = (1/2)mω<sup>2</sup>A<sup>2</sup> remains constant throughout the motion, confirming energy conservation in the absence of non-conservative forces.

concept_notes.heading: Damped Harmonic Motion
bullets: Real physical systems experience a resistive force proportional to velocity, represented as F<sub>d</sub> = -b(dx/dt).
The displacement equation for light damping (γ < ω<sub>0</sub>) is x(t) = A<sub>0</sub> e<sup>-γt</sup> cos(ω<sub>d</sub>t + φ), where γ = b/(2m) is the damping coefficient.
The damped angular frequency is given by ω<sub>d</sub> = √(ω<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> - γ<sup>2</sup>).

concept_notes.heading: Forced Oscillations and Resonance
bullets: A system driven by an external periodic force F(t) = F<sub>0</sub> cos(ωt) oscillates at the driving frequency ω after transient terms decay.
The steady-state amplitude depends strongly on the driving frequency and reaches a maximum when ω approaches the natural frequency ω<sub>0</sub>.
Resonance sharpness is determined by the quality factor Q = ω<sub>0</sub> / (2γ), where lower damping yields a higher peak amplitude.

derivations.title: Time Period of a Simple Pendulum
derivations.conditions: Amplitude of oscillation is small (θ << 1 radian) so that sin(θ) ≈ θ.
steps: Write the torque about the point of suspension: τ = -mg L sin(θ).
Equate torque to angular acceleration using moment of inertia I = mL<sup>2</sup>: mL<sup>2</sup> (d<sup>2</sup>θ/dt<sup>2</sup>) = -mg L sin(θ).
Apply small angle approximation to obtain the linear second-order differential equation: d<sup>2</sup>θ/dt<sup>2</sup> + (g/L)θ = 0.
Compare with standard SHM equation d<sup>2</sup>θ/dt<sup>2</sup> + ω<sup>2</sup>θ = 0 to identify ω = √(g/L).

derivations.title: Differential Equation of Damped Harmonic Oscillator
derivations.conditions: System subject to restoring force -kx and viscous damping force -b(dx/dt).
steps: Rearrange terms to form a homogeneous linear differential equation: m(d<sup>2</sup>x/dt<sup>2</sup>) + b(dx/dt) + kx = 0.
Divide by mass m and substitute ω<sup>2</sup><sub>0</sub> = k/m and 2γ = b/m: d<sup>2</sup>x/dt<sup>2</sup> + 2γ(dx/dt) + ω<sup>2</sup><sub>0</sub>x = 0.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Time and Velocity-Time Graphs in SHM
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Sine curve for displacement x(t) and cosine curve for velocity v(t) plotted on the same time axis, showing a phase difference of π/2 radians.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: When displacement is maximum (amplitude A), velocity is zero; when displacement is zero, velocity magnitude is maximum (ωA).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual MCQs regarding phase relationships between kinematic variables.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Amplitude vs Driving Frequency (Resonance Curve)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped curve of forced amplitude against driving frequency ω, with sharper peaks corresponding to lower damping coefficients.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Peak amplitude occurs near the natural frequency ω<sub>0</sub>; lower damping results in a significantly taller and narrower resonance peak.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct theoretical questions on sharpness of resonance and quality factor.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Portrait of Damped Oscillator (Phase Space)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A spiral converging inward toward the origin (0,0) in the v-x phase plane.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Both position and velocity decrease to zero over time due to continuous energy dissipation by the damping force.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced conceptual analysis in PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: A particle executing simple harmonic motion has a maximum displacement of 4 cm and a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate its maximum velocity.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: Amplitude A = 4 cm = 0.04 m, frequency f = 50 Hz.

solved_numericals.question: Find the length of a simple pendulum that has a time period of 2.0 seconds at a place where g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
solution_steps: Use the time period formula for a simple pendulum: T = 2π √(L/g).
Square both sides to solve for length L: T<sup>2</sup> = 4π<sup>2</sup>(L/g) ⇒ L = (T<sup>2</sup>g) / (4π<sup>2</sup>).

solved_numericals.question: A 0.5 kg mass is attached to a spring of stiffness 200 N/m and experiences a damping force with coefficient b = 4.0 kg/s. Determine the damped angular frequency.

assumptions_and_limitations: Hooke's law assumes elasticity is linear and springs do not exceed their elastic limit.
Simple pendulum derivations assume small angular displacements where sin(θ) ≈ θ and ignore mass of the string and air resistance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Acceleration in SHM is maximum when displacement is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: Acceleration is zero when displacement is zero, and maximum when displacement is at its peak amplitude.
common_misconceptions.why: Acceleration is given by a = -ω<sup>2</sup>x, making it directly proportional to displacement magnitude.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Total energy of a damped oscillator remains constant.
common_misconceptions.correct: Total energy decreases continuously with time in damped oscillations due to work done against non-conservative viscous forces.
common_misconceptions.why: Viscous damping dissipates mechanical energy into thermal energy.

quick_revision: In SHM, displacement, velocity, and acceleration are successively out of phase by π/2 radians.
Angular Frequency of Spring-Mass System: omega = sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}
Time Period of Simple Pendulum: T = 2pi sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}
